journal-v1.title: Ugrakshatriya-Pratinidhi, Volume I (1298 Bangabda)

journal-v2.title: Ugrakshatriya-Pratinidhi, Volume II (1299 Bangabda)
journal-v2.label: Original Bengali journal
journal-v2.detail: Owner-supplied scan: Ugrakshatriya_Pratinidhi_Vol_02.pdf. 167 PDF images, mostly spreads. The first image bears the second-volume label and year 1299 (1892–93), and begins Pratinidhir Atmakatha, the periodical’s account of itself. The report of the Ugrakshatriya Samiti’s sixth session, held on 17–18 Shraban 1299 (printed pp. 104–105, scan 53), lists the thirteen members present, the Samiti’s five aims, the transfer of the journal from its editor and proprietor, Srishchandra Ta, and a resolution against Risley’s account of the caste.
journal-v2.status: Owner-supplied PDF. Complete Pratinidhir Atmakatha (printed pp. 1–5) translated against the scans. Bengali OCR remains unreviewed; most of the volume is not translated. The Samiti report was read against the scan image on 8 October 2026; it has not been translated in full.

risley.title: H. H. Risley, The Tribes and Castes of Bengal, Vol. I (1891), pp. 12–13
risley.label: Colonial ethnography
risley.detail: The Aguri entry in the original digitised volume: cultivation and trade, seven named subdivisions, marriage sections, ritual practices and a historical distribution table. Internet Archive item TheTribesAndCastesOfBengal. The item’s OCR was consulted directly; census figures were not transcribed from its broken table.

mclane.title: John R. McLane, Land and Local Kingship in Eighteenth-Century Bengal (1993)
mclane.label: Historical scholarship
mclane.detail: Cambridge University Press, Cambridge South Asian Studies 53. Village “oligarchies” of dominant peasants, “typically Aguris, Kaibartas, or Sadgops” (pp. 54–55); “the raja of Burdwan’s naqdi or cash-paid army”, whose salaries fell from about Rs 4 lakh to just over Rs 1 lakh in 1761–67, and the 1760s table of 32,032 land-paid servants (pp. 117–118); chapter 6, “Mughal Burdwan and the rise of the Burdwan raj” (pp. 125–138): Burdwan as a Mughal garrison town, the Khatri origins of the Raj family, Abu Rai’s appointment (p. 134), Krishnaram Rai’s farman of 1695–96 (p. 137) and the revolt of 1696–97 (p. 129); Gopbhum, Oldham’s Khatri–Sadgop theory and the Aguris (pp. 157–160); the Raja’s unpaid troops and the battle of 29 December 1760 (pp. 183–185); Johnstone’s payroll cut and the 1767 reduction of the “naqdi or household guard” from 1,487 to 839 (p. 192); Kinloch’s 1787 halving of the zamindari troops to 1,000 (p. 263); 17,384 village paiks in 1794 (p. 271). Printed pp. 125–126 describe Burdwan’s embankments, flood damage and cultivators cutting banks for irrigation.
mclane.status: Read directly from the full Cambridge PDF (October 2026): pp. 54–55, 117–118, 125–138, 157–160, 183–185, 192, 263 and 271. McLane uses the Chandimangal, dated 1589 and quoted through Dimock and Inden’s translation, to treat the Aguris as older than the Khatris in Burdwan; this website records that reading and its limits on the Origins page. McLane does not connect the Aguris with the Raj’s naqdi (cash-paid) army or any other troops.

chakravarti-1970.title: Santosh Kumar Chakravarti, The History of the Relations of the Rajas of Burdwan and the East India Company during 1760–1832 (1970)
chakravarti-1970.label: Doctoral thesis · read in full
chakravarti-1970.detail: PhD thesis, Department of History, University of Burdwan, 1970; supervisor S. B. Chaudhuri. Shodhganga, CC BY-NC 4.0. Historical background, including the 1696 revolt (pp. 4–16); the action at the pass of the Banka river on 29 December 1760, from Captain White’s letter (pp. 22–24); the Raja’s 32,031 land-paid servants in 1766 (p. 162); the monthly allowance for the “Nugdean” or household troops, 1761–67, from the diwan’s representation of 1 October 1777 (p. 163); the 1767 establishment of 1,487 men, with those dismissed and retained (pp. 164–165); the abolition of the corps in March 1787 (p. 177); and the patni system on the Burdwan estate (chapter 4, pp. 123–154). McLane (1993) cites it as Chakrabarti, “History”.
chakravarti-1970.status: Read in full through the text layer of the Shodhganga PDFs in October 2026; figures and page numbers checked against that text. The thesis does not record the caste or origin of any of the Raja’s troops.

mukhopadhyay-2026.title: Kanchan Mukhopadhyay, Uneven Terrain: Society and Foodways in Rarh Bengal (2026)
mukhopadhyay-2026.label: Anthropology · preview consulted
mukhopadhyay-2026.detail: Routledge, 2026 (© Anthropological Survey of India). ISBN 9781041033073; DOI 10.4324/9781003625667. An ethnography of food and social relations in four Rarh villages in Paschim Medinipur, Jhargram, Bankura and Birbhum. The introduction, citing Porter’s 1931 census report (pp. 230–242), places agriculturist castes “such as Sadgop, Goala, and Aguri” in undivided Bardhaman and parts of Birbhum (p. 7).
mukhopadhyay-2026.status: Only the publisher’s preview (front matter, chapter 1 and references) was read. The single Aguri mention is a regional census observation; none of the four study villages is in Bardhaman.

bhaumik-2023.title: Sudarshana Bhaumik, The Changing World of Caste and Hierarchy in Bengal: Depiction from the Mangalkavyas c. 1700–1931 (2023)
bhaumik-2023.label: Historical scholarship · selected passages consulted
bhaumik-2023.detail: Routledge, first published 2023 (imprint page). ISBN 9780367557553; DOI 10.4324/9781003146186. Aguri literary references, settlement traditions, Gopbhum and Jana/Sutto divisions: pp. 48–49, with note 134 on p. 65; dominant cultivating castes and the Burdwan zamindari: pp. 166, 178; landholding and patni tenures: p. 198; the 1872 census description: p. 232; identity, sacred thread, Kulinism, census claims and subdivision reform: pp. 242, 244, 247, 252. Manasa, Dharma Thakur and Gajan: pp. 52, 74, 80, 82.
bhaumik-2023.status: Every Aguri and Ugra Kshatriya passage in the supplied book was located by full-text search and read in context; the rest of the book has not been reviewed. The Rajasthan–Man Singh migration account is presented as an attributed tradition alongside Dutta’s uncertainty about origins. Link opens the publisher’s book record. Its passages on Manasa and Dharma Thakur were read in context on 9 October 2026.

bhattacharya-1896.title: Jogendra Nath Bhattacharya, Hindu Castes and Sects (1896), contents p. x and pp. 156–158

bhattacharya-1896.detail: Calcutta: Thacker, Spink & Co. Part VII is headed “The Military Castes”; Chapter IX, “The Aguris of Bengal,” occupies pp. 156–158. chatterji-odbl.title: Suniti Kumar Chatterji, The Origin and Development of the Bengali Language (1926)
chatterji-odbl.label: Historical linguistics · sections consulted
chatterji-odbl.detail: Calcutta University Press, 1926, in two volumes. Surname derivations are cited by the author's own numbered sections: Dalui or Dalai from dalavai, dalapati, a commander of troops (§172); Bhar from bhata, bhrta, glossed “soldier, servant” (§173 and §683); Satra from samanta-raja and Maiti from mahanta (§273); Kongar or Koar from kumara (§284); the lineage affix -ja from jata (§435); Pakrasi from a village name (§455); Chaudhuri described as “a title or surname” (§514–515); Sasmal from sahasra-malla (§532). Also consulted: Bose from vasu (vol. I, p. 431, §233); Koṅgar / Kõar from kumāra and Sā̃tṛā from sāmanta-rāja / sāmanta-rāya (vol. I, p. 520). Ray from raja: vol. I, p. 590, §323.
chatterji-odbl.status: Section numbers taken from the digitised volumes held by this project; the machine-read text drops §515, so the Chaudhuri passage is cited as §514–515. These are the author's word histories, not histories of any family, and they do not establish the ancestry of anyone bearing a name.

risley-vol2.title: H. H. Risley, The Tribes and Castes of Bengal, Ethnographic Glossary, vol. II (1891)
risley-vol2.label: Colonial ethnographic glossary
risley-vol2.detail: The second volume of the glossary, covering headwords from L to Z, with Appendix I. Entries naming the Aguris directly: Samanta, “a chief … a title of Aguris, Brahmans, Khandaits, Rajputs, Sadgops, Telis, and some other castes”; Malla, “wrestler, a title of Khandaits in Orissa and of the Aguri or Ugrakshatri caste in Western Bengal”; Pan, “a title of Telis and Aguris in Western Bengal”; Rana, “a title of Aguris and Sutradhars”; Shahi Ugrakhatri, “a sub-caste of Aguris in Western Bengal bearing the title Shah”; Sandilya, a gotra of “the Aguri, Baidya, Brahman, Kamar, and Subarnabanik castes”; and the sub-castes Satsaikiya and Suta. Internet Archive identifier TheTribesAndCastesOfBengal_201509. Appendix I carries its own pagination.
risley-vol2.status: Evidence of what a colonial writer recorded in 1891, read from the machine-read text held by this project. Its caste ordering, origin theories and character stereotypes are not endorsed here. An entry records that a name was used; it does not establish descent, an ancestor's office, or that any community used the name first.

day-peasant-life.title: Lal Behari Day, Bengal Peasant Life (1916 reprint), preface and pp. 10, 31, 59, 82, 149, 204–207, 278–280
day-peasant-life.label: Literary primary source · page images checked
day-peasant-life.detail: First published as Govinda Sámanta (1874); new title Bengal Peasant Life (1878). The preface records the 1871 prize offered by Joy Kissen Mookerjea of Uttarpara and its award in 1874. The inspected 1916 reprint places Kanchanpur near Burdwan (chapter III, p. 10), identifies the Samanta brothers as Aguri (chapter V, p. 31), Natavara Samanta and Madhu Sinha through dialogue (IX, p. 59) and a Sen family through a matchmaker’s proposal (XIII, p. 82). Chapters XXIII (p. 149), XXX (pp. 204–207) and XLII (pp. 278–280) describe friendship across castes, the Navanna festival and the Aguri tenants’ protest against the zamindar. Archive scans n41, n69 and n92.
day-peasant-life.status: Pages 31, 59 and 82 read as page images on 21 September 2026. The preface and pp. 10, 149, 204–207 and 278–280 were read on 8 October 2026 in the item’s OCR text, using its running heads for page numbers; their page images have not been checked. Literary representation, not a verified pedigree or ethnography. Wording has not been collated against the 1874 edition.

moitra-2020.status: Passages on Day’s novel consulted online on 8 October 2026. Used for its reading of the novel, not as evidence of Aguri history.

togawa-1996.title: Masahiko Togawa, A Sakta-pitha in Bengal: Kingship, Caste and Sacrificial Organization in a Village Society (1996)
togawa-1996.label: Social anthropology · village fieldwork
togawa-1996.detail: PhD thesis, Social Anthropology, University of North Bengal, November 1996; supervisor Ajit K. Danda. Ethnography of the Jogadya temple at Kshiragram, Bardhaman. Chapter I (pp. 28–30): 1991 Census figures, caste household table, Jana and Suta Aguri households and nine title-defined lineages. Chapter II: temple land and the Raj. Chapter VI (pp. 131–165): Durga Puja of the Ugra Kshatriya localities, including a Caudhuri family document (pp. 157–158). Chapter V, pp. 116–122, also documents Nabanna, shared food, Pousalla and the temple’s pithe-bhumi rice plot.
togawa-1996.status: The Culture page directly cites Chapter I, p. 32 for Manasa puja as the Bagdis’ biggest festival at Kshiragram, with their own priest; this passage was checked against the thesis scan. Other accounts of lineages, temple land and rituals cite the published 2006 book (see Togawa 2006). The thesis remains a distinct source. Chapter V text independently checked on 11 October 2026 for the Food and Village Life article.

togawa-2006.title: Masahiko Togawa, An Abode of the Goddess: Kingship, Caste and Sacrificial Organization in a Bengal Village (2006)
togawa-2006.label: Social anthropology · village fieldwork
togawa-2006.detail: New Delhi: Manohar, 2006. ISBN 9788173046773. Published version of the author’s 1996 University of North Bengal thesis, based on fieldwork at Kshiragram, Mangalkot block, from January 1994 to April 1995. Introduction (pp. 13–26): the village, the Raj and the temple rebuilt about 1730. Chapter 2 (pp. 49–74): caste table, Jana and Suta Aguri households, the nine Ugra Kshatriya lineages and the Maharaja’s service lands. Chapter 4 (pp. 90–110): the Baishakh festival, including the sacred thread worn by the Datta and Samant representatives (p. 92). Chapter 6 (pp. 130–158): the Durga Pujas of the Ugra Kshatriya lineages and the Raychaudhuri lineage chart (pp. 147–150). Appendix 4 (pp. 194–195): temples founded by the Bardhaman Raj.
togawa-2006.status: Full book read. The study describes one village in 1994–95 and the author’s reconstruction of earlier practice; it is not a survey of all Aguri settlements.

saha-2026.title: Salini Saha, “Endangered cobras and conservation politics: Exploring multispecies encounters in agrarian landscapes of West Bengal” (2026)
saha-2026.label: Village ethnography · Bardhaman
saha-2026.detail: Journal of Political Ecology 33(1). DOI 10.2458/jpe.6439. Draws on the author’s Presidency University doctoral fieldwork (thesis: Fertility Worship and Monsoon among Agricultural Communities of Bardhaman, awarded 2023), with immersive fieldwork in 2018–2019. Printed p. 7 identifies Ugra Kshatriyas as Musharu’s dominant farming community, alongside Sadgops, Goalas, Namasudras and Bagdis. Printed pp. 6, 7, 11–12 and 14 describe village deities as markers of village identity, Musharu’s goddess Jhankeshwari and the Jhanglai cobras, snake worship in other east Bardhaman villages, and the growing public celebration of Jhankeshwari’s Shravan worship since 2021.
saha-2026.status: Original article read; pp. 5 and 7 checked as page images, and pp. 6, 11–12 and 14 in the extracted text. Describes a shared village culture, not practices exclusive to Aguris. The thesis is listed separately (Saha 2023).

saha-2023.title: Salini Saha, Fertility Worship and Monsoon among Agricultural Communities of Bardhaman (2023)
saha-2023.label: Doctoral thesis · village fieldwork
saha-2023.detail: PhD thesis, Department of Sociology, Presidency University, Kolkata; supervisor Sukanya Sarbadhikary. Title page dated 2023; deposited in the university repository in 2024. Fieldwork in villages around Bhatar and Mangalkot, Purba Bardhaman. Ugra Kshatriyas as more than half of the region’s farmers and agricultural labourers: pp. 13–14. Dharmaraj and Manasa in Bardhaman’s village religion, and household Manasa worship: pp. 87–90. Kal Rudra Shiva and Dharmapal at Bonkapasi, Mangalkot: pp. 119–122, 168–169, 191–198.
saha-2023.status: Read on 9 October 2026 by machine OCR of the repository’s chapter files, which are page scans; the cited passages were read in context. The villages studied have mixed populations, and the thesis does not single out any practice as Aguri. The 2026 journal article drawn from it is listed separately (Saha 2026).

klass-1978.title: Morton Klass, From Field to Factory: Community Structure and Industrialization in West Bengal (1978)
klass-1978.label: Social anthropology · Burdwan district
klass-1978.detail: Philadelphia: Institute for the Study of Human Issues. Fieldwork 1970–1975 in “Gondogram” (a pseudonym), Asansol subdivision, Burdwan district, studying how a nearby factory changed economic transactions, social relations and religious practice.
klass-1978.status: Bibliographic record and abstract consulted through the eHRAF World Cultures catalogue. The book was not read; no Aguri-specific finding is attributed to it.

ruud-1994.title: Arild Engelsen Ruud, “Land and Power: The Marxist Conquest of Rural Bengal” (1994)
ruud-1994.label: Political anthropology · Burdwan villages
ruud-1994.detail: Modern Asian Studies 28(2), pp. 357–380. DOI 10.1017/S0026749X00012440. Examines how the CPI(M) built rural support in the late 1960s through an alliance across peasant strata. Part of Ruud’s research in Burdwan district, also presented in his LSE PhD thesis “Socio-cultural changes in rural West Bengal” (1995), based on two Burdwan villages, and in Poetics of Village Politics (Oxford University Press, New Delhi, 2003).
ruud-1994.status: The earlier site review consulted the publisher’s abstract. The Konar profile now follows the historical and field-based discussion cited in the supplied bilingual biography; its linked full text was not independently rechecked during this update. Ruud’s Aguri material elsewhere is cited from his 2003 book.

ruud-2003.title: Arild Engelsen Ruud, Poetics of Village Politics: The Making of West Bengal’s Rural Communism (2003)
ruud-2003.label: Political anthropology · Burdwan villages
ruud-2003.detail: New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2003. Fieldwork in 1992–93 in two adjacent villages of Raina I block, Dakshin Damodar, Burdwan, given the fictitious names Udaynala and Gopinathpur. Aguris (“Uggra-Kshatriya”) are Gopinathpur’s dominant caste: population and land table, 1993 (pp. 16–17); the Mandal family and village leadership, 1953–77 (pp. 36–41, 52–53); landownership by caste about 1960 (pp. 115–116); education (p. 86); kin in service and business (pp. 84–85); census shares for Raina and the district (p. 123, n. 21–22 on p. 149); Dasarathi Tah as Raina’s MLA (p. 21).
ruud-2003.status: Chapters 2–5 read in the supplied scan, with all Aguri passages located by full-text search. Village and personal names in the book are the author’s; the villages are deliberately disguised and should not be identified with real places.

peterson-1910.title: J. C. K. Peterson, Bengal District Gazetteers: Burdwan (1910)
peterson-1910.label: Colonial district gazetteer
peterson-1910.detail: Calcutta: Bengal Secretariat Book Depot, 222 pp. Digitised by the Gokhale Institute of Politics and Economics. On p. 22 the gazetteer states that Aguris, “by their own admission”, arose from unions between Burdwan Khatris and Gopbhum Sadgops within the previous two hundred years, repeating Oldham’s explanation. Pages 56–57 describe the worship of Manasa and Dharmaraj in the district, quoting R. C. Dutt on Manasa’s origins.
peterson-1910.status: Read from the digitised copy in October 2026. The p. 22 passage was checked against the page image; the pages cited on the Origins page (pp. 27, 28, 31 and 32) were read in its text layer. A colonial assertion reported here as a disputed claim, not as established history. The Manasa and Dharmaraj passages (pp. 56–57) were read in its text layer on 9 October 2026.

bhattacharyya-1953.title: Asutosh Bhattacharyya, “Dharma Worship in West Bengal”, in A. Mitra, The Tribes and Castes of West Bengal (1953), pp. 351–360
bhattacharyya-1953.label: Folklore study · Census 1951
bhattacharyya-1953.detail: Census 1951, West Bengal. Calcutta: West Bengal Government Press, 1953, pp. 351–360; based on the author’s Bangla Mangal Kavyer Itihas (2nd edn, 1950), chapter IV. The area and spread of the cult (p. 351); a Dharma Thakur kept as the tutelary deity of an Aguri (Ugra Kshatriya) family at Khudkuri, Khandaghosh police station, Burdwan district, worshipped daily by a Brahman with boiled rice and put out in the sun in drought (pp. 352–353, 359); Dom and Brahman priests (pp. 352–353); the season of the annual worship (p. 354); earlier theories of Dharma’s origin and the author’s reading of him as a primitive sun-god (pp. 358–360).
bhattacharyya-1953.status: Read on 9 October 2026 from the North Bengal University repository scan (PDF pp. 359–368) by machine OCR; p. 352 was checked against the page image. The Khudkuri account describes one household around 1950. The argument about origins is the author’s interpretation, including his disputed derivation of the name Dharma from Dom.

bakshi-2014.title: Aparajita Bakshi, “Contextualising Land Reform in West Bengal: An Interview with Benoy Konar” (2014)
